strengths: The paper provides a clear and interesting analysis of why Prefix-Tuning underperforms on modern LLMs, refuting the common belief that PT cannot alter attention patterns (Figure 2, CKA/REEF analysis in Appendix B), and articulating a plausible prefix/input significance tradeoff via the decomposition in Equation (4).

The proposed method (PT+) is simple, well-motivated, and connects nicely to prior work on linearized attention (kernel approximation of prefix terms), with a useful 'unified view' section that positions context-based PEFT methods along a spectrum and could guide future method design.

Evaluation goes beyond a single setting: few-shot classification on multiple datasets, IID/OOD Pareto analysis, scaling across data rounds, two model architectures (MHA vs. GQA), and integration with SFT/DPO/SimPO alignment pipelines.
PT+ reportedly matches or exceeds LoRA on several benchmarks while remaining a context-based method, which, if reliable, is a meaningful result for the PEFT community.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the final architecture (Eq. 8) reduces to adding a query-dependent bias term phi(q_i)^T M to the attention output, which is closely related to existing bias/modulation-style PEFT methods (e.g., (IA)^3, bias tuning, and the linearized-attention construction of [4] that the authors themselves build on). The main contribution is more a recombination of known ideas than a fundamentally new technique.

The headline claim in the abstract/intro is inconsistent and overstated: the abstract says PT+ is 'on par with LoRA', while the contributions claim an 'average absolute improvement of 8.1% over LoRA and 29.4% over Prefix-Tuning' — averages that are inflated by Prefix-Tuning's very poor baseline numbers rather than consistent gains over LoRA.

Evaluation breadth is thinner than presented: 'BigBench' is actually a single task (Date Understanding), so IID results cover only three datasets; and no code release is mentioned, hurting reproducibility.

Several results raise concerns about experimental fairness or setup: full fine-tuning dramatically underperforms all PEFT methods (e.g., 32.7 vs. 45.2 on GoEmotions; 38.8 vs. 71.2 on BigBench), and Prefix-Tuning's 5.6% on GoEmotions is anomalously low; a single fixed learning rate (2e-5) and 4000 steps for all methods suggests baselines may be under-tuned.

Missing ablations and baselines: the 'Choice 1 vs Choice 2' ablation (Eq. 9) is proposed but never evaluated; the feature map phi is fixed to ELU with no comparison to alternatives; trainable phi, M's dimensionality, and prefix-length sensitivity for PT+ are unexplored; standard PEFT baselines such as P-Tuning v2, (IA)^3, bitfit, or VeRA are absent; parameter counts of PT+ vs. LoRA r=64 are not clearly reported.

The causal argument that the prefix/input tradeoff is the reason PT fails is supported only indirectly (attention maps from one example, eigenvalue spectra, CKA similarities); no intervention experiment directly validates that removing the alpha scaling causes the observed performance gains.

The alignment results (Table 2) show small win-rate differences (e.g., 0.76 vs 0.49 for SFT) from single runs with no statistical significance testing, and the DPO-vs-SimPO observation is speculative.

Presentation issues: Figure 1 is referenced before it appears while Figure 2 is shown first, several typos ('differed to Appendix', 'Accuracys'), and Remark 2's memory-perspective framing is qualitative without supporting experiments.

strengths: The motivating question is relevant: understanding why Prefix-Tuning degrades on modern LLMs and whether context-based PEFT can be revived is of genuine interest to the PEFT community.

The paper attempts a principled derivation (Eqs. 5-8) connecting prefix-tuning to an externalized bias module, and the 'unified view' (Section 5.2) framing context-based PEFT as a sequence of design decisions is a nice expository device.

The experimental scope covers multiple settings: few-shot adaptation, IID/OOD Pareto analysis, scaling across data rounds, MHA vs. GQA models, and alignment objectives (SFT/DPO/SimPO), which is more breadth than many PEFT papers attempt.
Diagnostic analyses (attention maps, CKA similarity, eigenvalue spectra) go beyond pure benchmark reporting and attempt to build a mechanistic story.
weaknesses: Novelty is questionable. After all the intermediate steps are discarded (lambda absorbed, the N term removed, kernel map fixed to ELU), the final method (Eq. 8) is simply adding a query-dependent bias phi(q_i)^T M to the attention output — i.e., essentially a per-layer MLP-style adapter on attention output, very close to existing work such as (IA)^3, parallel adapters, and the cited linearization work [4] that already proposed the bias term b_1. The framing as a 'Prefix-Tuning' generalization feels like packaging rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The paper's own construction is not ablated. The authors explicitly introduce an intermediate variant (Eq. 9, keeping the prefix inside the attention head with the trainable matrix) and a two-way design space (Choice 1 vs. Choice 2), but never run the ablation separating them. The Discussion admits 'the design of our method has yet to be thoroughly ablated.' For a paper whose central contribution is an architectural design choice, this is a serious omission.

Baseline results raise calibration concerns. Full fine-tuning at 38.8% on BigBench vs. 71.2% for PT+, and LoRA (r=64) at 26.8% on GoEmotions with Qwen2.5, are implausibly weak for standard PEFT setups and contradict widely reported behavior where LoRA roughly matches full fine-tuning. These anomalies make the headline claims ('8.1% average absolute improvement over LoRA') unreliable, and the abstract simultaneously claims 'on par with LoRA,' which is internally inconsistent with the introduction's '8.1% improvement.' No hyperparameter search protocol for baselines is described.

Evaluation scope is narrow and somewhat misleading. 'BigBench' is actually a single task (Date Understanding); all main evaluations are classification-style generative QA. There are no standard PEFT benchmarks (e.g., SuperNaturalInstructions, commonsense reasoning suites), no perplexity or generation-quality evaluation, and no measurement of the actual efficiency (training time, memory, inference overhead) that motivates PEFT in the first place — despite Remark 2's parameter-efficiency claims.

The causal analysis motivating the method is weak. The claim that 'inability to alter attention patterns is not why PT fails' rests on qualitative attention heatmaps from single examples at one layer, and the 'tradeoff between prefix and input significance' argument is largely an algebraic restatement of softmax normalization rather than empirically established causation.

Writing and presentation are below the bar for a top venue: figures are referenced out of order (Figure 2 appears before Figure 1), undefined notation (s'_j in Eq. 4), grammatical errors ('we aims to study', 'differed to Appendix', 'perform under compared'), and Figure 3 lacks clear axis interpretation. No code release is mentioned, which harms reproducibility for a methods paper.

Supporting claims are overreached: Remark 1 asserts PT+ 'has the ability to be extremely expressive, matching methods such as full fine-tuning and LoRA' without evidence; the CKA analysis (Table 3) conflates representation shift with expressiveness in a speculative manner.

strengths: The core motivation is interesting and clearly argued: the paper provides an empirical investigation (attention maps, CKA/REEF similarity, eigenvalue spectrum analysis) into why Prefix-Tuning underperforms on modern LLMs, and challenges the prior claim that PT cannot alter attention patterns.

The decomposition of the prefix-tuned attention output (Eq. 4) into an input term plus prefix-weighted term gives a clean, interpretable framing of the prefix/input significance tradeoff, and the derivation from PT to PT+ is transparent.

Evaluation covers multiple dimensions: few-shot IID accuracy across three classification tasks, IID/OOD Pareto tradeoff analysis, data-scaling rounds, both MHA and GQA models, and practical alignment experiments (SFT/DPO/SimPO with AlpacaEval 2), which is broader than a typical proof-of-concept PEFT paper.
The 'unified view' of context-based methods (Section 5.2) and explicit statement of design choices is a useful contribution for practitioners constructing context-based PEFT methods.
The paper is honest about being a proof of concept and about limitations (naive ELU feature map, limited ablations, resource constraints).
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the final PT+ update (Eq. 8) reduces to adding a trainable query-dependent bias term φ(q_i)ᵀM to each attention output, which is architecturally very close to existing additive/scaled modifications such as (IA)^3, simple linear adapters on the attention output, and the linearization approaches the authors themselves cite [4, 13, 23]. The paper does not compare against (IA)^3 or similar lightweight alternatives, making it hard to isolate what is genuinely new versus a rebranding of a known bias-plus-attention design.

The causal story is not fully validated. Section 4.2 argues the prefix/input significance tradeoff is the reason PT fails, but the evidence is largely correlational (attention visualizations, CKA shifts). There is no experiment showing that the tradeoff (rather than optimization difficulty, prefix length sensitivity, or other factors) is the actual cause of PT's underperformance, nor a direct intervention isolating α.

Evaluation raises concerns: (1) BigBench is reduced to a single task (Date Understanding) yet reported simply as 'BigBench'; (2) Table 1 shows full fine-tuning at 38.8% on BigBench (LLaMA2), far below LoRA (67.4%) and even ICL—suggesting the full-FT baseline is mistuned or unstable, which undermines baseline credibility; (3) no standard deviations or significance tests are reported for the few-shot results despite five-round sampling; (4) only two models and small classification-style tasks; key PEFT baselines like (IA)^3, BitFit, prompt tuning are absent.

Missing or inconsistent experimental details: the CKA experiment (Appendix B.3) evaluates on TruthfulQA while the surrounding experiments use GoEmotions/Banking77, without explanation; parameter counts for PT+ versus LoRA (r=64) and PT (m=32) are only loosely matched ('approximately'); the claim of an 8.1% average gain over LoRA coexists uneasily with the abstract's 'on par with LoRA' framing.

Ablations are insufficient for the paper's own central design claims: Section 5.2 argues Choices 1 and 2 can be applied independently (Eq. 9), but no experiment ablates them separately, and the fixed choice of φ(x)=elu(x) is untested against alternatives that the Remark 1 expressiveness argument depends on.

Writing and presentation issues: several typos and grammatical errors ('underperformed' phrasing, 'results in Table 4 confirms', 'leave results on more datasets in Appendix A.2' vs. actual A.2 content), Figure 1 and Figure 2 discussion is thin, and the analysis relies on single-example attention heatmaps which are not statistically meaningful.
No code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility of a method whose implementation details (how M is initialized and shaped per head/layer) matter significantly.

strengths: The paper offers a clear and empirically supported diagnosis of why Prefix-Tuning struggles on modern LLMs: the softmax normalization inside attention heads creates a tradeoff between prefix and input contribution (Section 4.2, Eq. 3). The revisit of the Petrov et al. (2023) claim that PT cannot alter attention patterns, with supporting CKA/REEF and attention-map analyses (Appendix B), is a useful and non-trivial empirical contribution.

The proposed method is derived transparently through a sequence of design choices (Eqs. 4-7), and the paper explicitly frames itself as a proof of concept with a unified view (Section 5.3) that could guide future context-based PEFT design.

Evaluation breadth is respectable: diagnostic classification (IID + OOD with Pareto analysis across checkpoints), data-scaling rounds, both MHA and GQA architectures, feature-map ablations, LoRA rank sweeps, parameter/memory/throughput/latency comparisons, and application-scale experiments (SFT/DPO/SimPO alignment, CFT math reasoning).

Multiple diagnostic experiments (eigenvalue spectrum of the bias term, CKA similarity, prefix-length sensitivity) give mechanistic insight beyond raw benchmark numbers, and the appendix is candid about limitations.
weaknesses: Novelty of the final architecture is questionable. After the derivation, the prefix has disappeared entirely and PMT (Eq. 7) reduces to adding a query-conditioned bias phi(q_i)^T M to attention output — essentially a parallel low-rank adapter with an ELU/GELU nonlinearity. The framing as 'Prefix-Tuning' is stretched; the connection to Chen et al. (2024) is acknowledged but the delta over that prior work is modest.

Overclaiming relative to the evidence. The abstract and introduction claim 'an average absolute improvement of 8.1% over LoRA', but Table 1 shows mixed results (e.g., LoRA beats PMT on GoEmotions for Qwen2.5: 37.8 vs 37.3). The aggregation behind 8.1% is not clearly defined.

Suspicious/under-explained results in the math experiments (Table 3): LoRA accuracy is completely flat across 10K and 50K samples (47.5/47.5, 16.7/16.7) while PMT jumps substantially, which suggests possible baseline under-tuning or evaluation artifacts. Differences on AIME24 (13.3 vs 10.0 etc.) correspond to only ~1 problem on a 30-item test set, yet no statistical significance or variance is reported for these or for Table 1.

Missing important baselines: the paper cites DePT, ADePT, P-Tuning v2, and GaLore as relevant modern PEFTs but only compares against LoRA, LoRA+, full FT, and vanilla Prefix-Tuning. Given the claim that PMT is competitive with 'state-of-the-art' PEFTs, comparisons against improved context-based PEFTs are needed.

Key derivation steps are hand-wavy. Removing the convex combination weight lambda ('can be absorbed into trainable weights') and the normalization term N ('no longer meaningful for regularization') is asserted rather than justified; the equivalence between the Eq. 4 objective and Eq. 7 is not established. The tradeoff analysis in Section 4.2 is also qualitative rather than a quantitative predictive theory.

Inconsistencies and sloppiness: Section 5.2/6.1 states heavier feature-map parameterizations (e.g., MLPs) are 'left to future work to preserve parameter efficiency', yet Table 2 already reports an 'MLP Kernel' variant (which performs worse); typos ('expri-ments', 'underperform', 'overperform'); Figure 3 axes are unlabeled and hard to interpret; the CKA section switches evaluation dataset to TruthfulQA without explanation.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, hyperparameters for the application-scale experiments (DPO/SimPO win rates, CFT training) are sparse, and it is unclear how phi is applied in GQA models where keys/values are shared across query heads.

The 'memory' interpretation (Remark 2) is mostly rhetorical — M is simply a trainable matrix, and the claimed advantages (interpretability, test-time adaptation) of context-based methods are arguably lost once the prefix is replaced by phi(q)M, undermining the motivating narrative that Prefix-Tuning's unique benefits are being preserved.

strengths: The paper is clearly written at a conceptual level and the diagnostic framing (rewriting prefix-tuned attention as a convex combination of input attention and prefix bias, Eq. 3) is a clean way to articulate the prefix/input contribution tradeoff.
The method is simple and cheap: a query-conditioned bias term φ(q_i)^T M attached outside the softmax, with negligible overhead compared to LoRA (Tables 5-6).

The empirical coverage is broad for a proof of concept: few-shot classification, OOD (Pareto) analysis, preference alignment (SFT/DPO/SimPO), and math reasoning (CFT), plus spectrum/CKA analyses that probe the mechanism.
The authors are candid about the proof-of-concept nature of the work and honestly discuss limitations (model scale, feature map choice, compute constraints).
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The final method (Eq. 7) reduces to o_i = softmax_attention(q,k,v) + φ(q_i)^T M, i.e., adding a trainable query-conditioned linear adapter to the attention output. This is essentially a lightweight parallel adapter and is closely related to existing techniques such as (IA)^3, IA3-style rescaling adapters, Chen et al. (2024) (which the authors build on), Munkhdalai et al. (2024), and residual/parallel adapter literature. The 'prefix-tuning' framing and the lengthy derivation from Eq. 4-7 obscure that the end result is a well-known family of additive adapters; the paper does not adequately position itself against or ablate against these closest relatives.

The central causal claim is under-supported. The argument that prefix-tuning fails due to the softmax-induced tradeoff between prefix and input contribution is supported only indirectly (attention heatmaps, CKA similarity, eigenvalue spectra). No intervention experiment directly isolates the softmax normalization as the culprit—for example, comparing prefix-tuning with a fixed convex combination (Eq. 4, with λ swept) vs. standard PT at matched parameters. The λ mechanism, which is the only direct test of the hypothesis, is dropped from the final architecture and never empirically validated.

Experimental setup raises fairness and validity concerns. Full fine-tuning performs far below PEFT methods (e.g., 32.7% vs. 45.2% for PMT on GoEmotions; 38.8% vs. 71.2% on BigBench), which is atypical and strongly suggests under-tuned hyperparameters for the strongest baseline. Similarly, the enormous gaps in Table 3 (62.5% vs. 23.9% on Minerva-Math at 50K) exceed what a PEFT-vs-PEFT comparison should plausibly produce without controlling optimization details. With such unexplained anomalies, the headline claims ('8.1% average improvement over LoRA') are not credible at face value.

Baselines are narrow. Only LoRA (one rank), LoRA+, and vanilla prefix-tuning are compared. Modern, directly relevant PEFTs—DoRA, PiSSA, rsLoRA, VeRA, IA^3, DePT/ADePT (which the related work itself cites)—are missing, despite claims of competitiveness with 'modern PEFTs'.

Scale and scope are limited for the claims made. All experiments use 3B-7B models, few-shot classification with as few as 6 training examples, and only one BIG-bench task (Date Understanding) is labeled 'BigBench'. The paper argues prefix-tuning fails specifically at depth/scale, yet never evaluates at the scale where that thesis matters (>13B).

Writing and presentation quality is below the bar for a top venue: inconsistent naming (BigBench/Dbpedia/DBpedia), broken references ('table 2', 'figure 2' lowercase, missing spaces), a citation to a GitHub issue ('schrieffer-z, 2024') in the main text, typos ('expri-ments', 'Accuracys'), and an abstract that claims PMT 'consistently outperforms existing Prefix-Tuning methods' while the contribution bullets pivot to LoRA comparisons.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is stated, key implementation details (where exactly M is placed per layer/head, initialization of M, how d_φ is set, hyperparameter search protocol per method) are missing, which matters greatly given the sensitivity the authors themselves report to the choice of activation φ.

Self-positioning tension: the paper motivates a fix to prefix-tuning's scaling failure but the final method no longer retains any prefix structure (the prefix vectors s_j, W_K, W_V interactions are fully replaced by a free matrix M), so the connection to prefix-tuning is more rhetorical than architectural; this weakens both the scientific narrative and the significance of the contribution.

strengths: The paper asks a relevant and somewhat underexplored question: why does Prefix-Tuning fail on modern LLMs, and can its core idea be rescued? The diagnosis of a softmax-induced tradeoff between prefix and input contribution (Section 4.2) is clearly motivated and supported by the decomposition of Eq. 2/3.

The proposed PrefixMemory-Tuning is simple and well-grounded: the derivation from prefix-tuning to the query-conditioned bias term φ(q)ᵀM (Eqs. 4-7) is transparent, and the 'unified view' of design choices (Section 5.3) is a useful contribution for future work on context-based PEFT.

Experiments cover several regimes: few-shot classification across two models (MHA vs GQA), OOD generalization via Pareto plots, data-scaling rounds, preference alignment (SFT/DPO/SimPO), and math reasoning via CFT. Diagnostic analyses (attention maps, eigenvalue spectra, CKA similarity) give reasonable mechanistic evidence that PMT differs from PT and LoRA.
The paper is honest about being a proof of concept, includes explicit limitations (Appendix E), licenses, and LLM-usage disclosure, which supports reproducibility and ethics standards.
Efficiency analysis (Tables 5-6) shows the method is training- and inference-efficient relative to PT, addressing a practical concern.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the final architecture (Eq. 7) reduces to standard attention plus a trainable query-conditioned linear bias φ(q)ᵀM per layer. This is functionally close to parallel adapters, (IA)³, or the linearization of prompts in Chen et al. (2024) and Mercat et al. (2024), which the paper builds on. The kernel-approximation framing obscures rather than clarifies that the contribution is essentially adding a learned low/medium-rank adapter at the attention output. Comparison against parallel adapters or (IA)³, which would isolate what is genuinely new, is missing.

The central causal claim—that PT underperforms specifically because of the prefix/input contribution tradeoff inside softmax—is supported only indirectly. The diagnostic evidence (attention deviation with prefix length, CKA similarity) is correlational; there is no direct intervention (e.g., manipulating λ in Eq. 4) demonstrating that removing the softmax coupling, rather than simply increasing parameter expressivity, drives the gains. PMT's advantage may largely be 'more expressive adapter', not 'decoupled prefix'.

Evaluation gaps and inconsistencies: the striking math results (e.g., Minerva-Math 62.5 vs 23.9 at 50K samples) are reported without variance over seeds and appear surprisingly large, warranting verification. AlpacaEval 2 results are reported as 'win-rate deltas' without clarifying whether length-controlled win rates are used, a known pitfall. Table 1 shows full fine-tuning severely underperforming few-shot LoRA (38.8% vs 67.4% on BigBench), which suggests possible overfitting/protocol issues that are not discussed.

Missing important baselines: context-based PEFT methods discussed in related work (DePT, ADePT, P-Tuning v2) and lightweight alternatives like (IA)³ or VeRA are cited but not compared, weakening the claim that PMT is competitive with state-of-the-art PEFTs.

Scale and generality limitations: all main experiments use 3B-7B models and few-shot settings with one example per class; the paper's own limitations section concedes that abundant-data and >70B regimes were not tested, yet the abstract/introduction claim competitiveness with 'modern PEFTs' and 'potential extension to state-of-the-art' that outstrip the evidence.

Ablations are thin: only ELU vs GELU vs an MLP kernel are tested for φ; the effect of M's dimensionality, per-layer vs selective placement, and interaction with existing regularization are unexplored. Several design decisions (dropping N, absorbing λ) are justified heuristically rather than empirically.

Presentation issues reduce polish: typos ('outperform baselines', 'expri-ments', inconsistent capitalization of method names), an unexplained reference '(schrieffer-z, 2024)' (a GitHub issue) as a citation for a technical claim, and no statement of code release, which limits reproducibility.
